title: Analogy Placement — First Introduction Only
description: An analogy belongs where a concept is met for the FIRST time, and nowhere else. Every slide declares a `role`; the rule is an exact biconditional: analogy present iff role == concept_intro. An analogy on an advantages/disadvantages slide, a reasoning slide, a comparison table, a mechanism walk-through, an application slide, a summary or a worked example costs page space and teaches nothing — it was being generated only because an older rule demanded all six fields on every slide.
criterion: Every concept_intro slide has exactly one analogy; every other role has none. Roles are honestly assigned: at most half the slides may be concept_intro. Slide `role` is present and valid on every slide.

rubric.5: Analogies exactly on the first-introduction slides, none anywhere else, roles honestly assigned.
rubric.3: One misplaced or one missing analogy.
rubric.1: Multiple analogies outside first introductions, missing roles, or concept_intro over-used to keep them.

input.analogy: Four cars entering a narrow crossroads from four sides, each blocking the next — just as four processes each hold one resource and wait for the next.

cases.rationale: First introduction, one analogy, explicit tie-back.

input.analogy: Like booking all your train tickets before starting a trip — just as requesting every resource up front avoids waiting later.

cases.rationale: An advantages/limitations slide needs no analogy; the concept is already on the table.

input.analogy: Like a bank lending only what it can still cover — just as the algorithm grants a request only if a safe sequence remains.

cases.rationale: A worked example teaches by tracing real figures. An analogy on top of it is decoration.

input.concept: Why circular wait must be broken
input.analogy: Like a queue at a canteen counter — just as ordering resources removes the cycle.

cases.rationale: Reasoning slides explain why; the analogy adds length, and a queue is also the wrong structural match for a cycle.
